paper_title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Two snapshots of room, one facing the window and one facing the door, are enough to walk through it in the mind: stand by the sofa, face the shelf, and the window is on the left (Figure 1). Behind this lie two operations: assembling the snapshots into one model of the room, and mentally rotating that model to the new standpoint (Shepard and Metzler, 1971). As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) (Huang et al., 2026a; Aneja et al., 2026; Qwen Team, 2026a) advance rapidly in visual understanding and reasoning, real-world tasks such as embodied AI (Wu et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026a), autonomous driving (Luo et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b), and extended reality (Yang et al., 2026c; Li and Yao, 2026) increasingly hinge on such spatial intelligence. Despite its importance, spatial intelligence remains major bottleneck for MLLMs (Wang et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), requiring the model to mentally construct coherent 3D scene rather than merely recognize 2D visual patterns. As Figure 2a illustrates, existing approaches generally fall into two paradigms: (i) External-geometry methods construct the scene outside the model, via 3D reconstruction and rendering (Zhang et al., 2026f; Yang et al., 2025; Cho et al., 2026) or an attached geometry encoder (Wu et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). While providing explicit geometry, they fail to internalize spatial capability and incur high inference latency (Li et al., 2026g,e). (ii) Spatial fine-tuning methods aim to train the MLLM to construct the scene internally, with supervision progressing from the output text alone (Li et al., 2026d; Yang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026f) to latent states aligned with 3D geometry (Chen et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026a; Wang and Huang, 2026; Oi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). This paradigm has drawn growing attention for its promise of internalizing spatial capability within the model itself. However, the evidence for this promise rests largely on end-task accuracy. We therefore introduce spatial probes, extending recent analyses of the spatial representations inside MLLMs (Shi et al., 2026b), to decode the scene model holds internally. Our probes reveal that, despite substantial gains in accuracy, spatially fine-tuned models retain two persistent deficiencies in spatial capability, as illustrated in Figure 2b. (i) Limited multi-view fusion: these models encode each view well but in isolation, and the views are barely fused into coherent scene. (ii) Incomplete perspective transformation: as in base models (Shi et al., 2026b), their internal representation still largely fails to follow when the reasoning shifts to new viewpoint. This mismatch raises natural question: Research Question How can an MLLM truly internalize spatial capability, assembling its views into one scene and rotating that scene to new viewpoint, as humans do? To address this question, we introduce S-MIND, framework that endows an MLLM with an internal scene representation, built from its input views and transformed as its reasoning unfolds. (I) Multiview fusion. S-MIND introduces compact set of spatial tokens whose hidden states consolidate the views into unified 3D scene, encoding both the geometry each image observes and the pose of each camera in shared coordinate frame. (II) Perspective transformation. With the views fused into one scene, adopting new viewpoint reduces to re-expressing that scene in different frame of reference. Whenever the reasoning shifts to new viewpoint, the model therefore re-emits the spatial tokens, which now encode the fused scene as observed from that viewpoint, and conditions its subsequent reasoning on them. By training the model to construct and manipulate an entire 3D scene, S-MIND internalizes genuine spatial capability rather than superficial heuristics. Extensive evaluations across four spatial reasoning benchmarks and two model scales demonstrate the effectiveness of S-MIND. (I) Strong performance: S-MIND reaches an average accuracy of up to 74.03%, surpassing the strongest fine-tuned baseline by 6.76 points and the best released spatial reasoning model by 19.11 points, and rivaling frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45) and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97). (II) Internalized spatial capability: At the representation level, S-MIND 2 Figure 2: Internalizing spatial capability in MLLMs. The top panel (a) contrasts the two existing paradigms for spatial intelligence with S-MIND: external-geometry methods build the scene outside the model via 3D reconstruction; spatial fine-tuning improves the answers without forming coherent internal scene; and S-MIND explicitly fuses the views into an internal scene and rotates it as the reasoning proceeds. The bottom panel (b) shows topdown views of the internal scenes decoded on two questions: the spatially fine-tuned baseline (Qwen3.5-4B + SFT, read through the spatial probes) neither fuses the two views nor turns the scene to the stated viewpoint, whereas S-MIND does both. Dashed circles mark the baselines errors. overcomes both deficiencies. Multi-view fusion raises the recovery rate of cross-view 3D points from at most 16.02% for the baselines to 65.11%, and perspective transformation lifts the accuracy of locating points relative to new viewpoint from at most 37.28% to 82.17%. (III) Efficient and internalized reasoning: Requiring no tool calls, S-MIND runs roughly 100 faster than an externalgeometry agent on the same backbone. Moreover, spatial capability is instilled into the backbone through the spatial tokens during training: even with all of them withheld at inference, S-MIND loses only 2.37 points and still leads the strongest baseline on its backbone by 5.28 points. Contributions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Representation-Level Diagnosis. Through our spatial probes, we identify two deficiencies in the spatial capability of current MLLMs, limited multi-view fusion and incomplete perspective transformation, which persist even after spatial fine-tuning substantially improves their accuracy. Practical Solution. We propose S-MIND, which addresses both deficiencies through spatial tokens that consolidate the views into unified 3D scene and are re-emitted at each viewpoint shift to re-express that scene in the new frame. Experimental Validation. We validate S-MIND across four benchmarks and two model scales, showing that it internalizes spatial capability, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spatial reasoning models, rivals frontier general models, and attains high inference efficiency.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: External-Geometry Methods. External-geometry methods compute the scene outside the MLLM and supply it as input. Tool-based designs invoke specialist modules at inference: some build and operate on an explicit scene representation, such as 3D reconstruction, an object-level abstraction, or vector sketch (Zhang et al., 2026f; Cho et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026); others synthesize views from new standpoints using generative models (Yang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026c) or warp visual tokens toward them (Lee et al., 2026). Encoder-based designs instead integrate geometry into the architecture, pairing the visual encoder with feed-forward reconstruction model such as VGGT (Wang et al., 2025) and fusing their features (Wu et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026); subsequent work refines where and how these features are injected (Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026c). However, both designs offload scene construction to external modules, failing to internalize genuine spatial capability while incurring extra inference overhead (Li et al., 2026g,e). S-MIND keeps the geometry but moves it from inference into training, where it teaches the model itself to fuse the views and transform the scene. Spatial Fine-Tuning Methods. Spatial fine-tuning methods train the MLLM to form the scene internally, with no geometry at inference. Most methods shape only what the model says: they scale up spatial instruction data (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026b,a), train with progressive curricula, process-level rewards, or interaction trajectories (Li et al., 2026d,f; Yao et al., 2026), elicit textual cognitive maps or cross-view alignments before the answer (Wang et al., 2026b; Hua et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2026), or distill tool-using agents and privileged geometry (Li et al., 2026g,e). growing body of work, closer in spirit to latent reasoning (Hao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2026d), shapes what the model holds instead: it aligns latent states with 3D foundation models or across views (Chen et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026a; Wang and Huang, 2026; Oi et al., 2026), or adds dedicated tokens for positions, directions, and an observers orientation (Li et al., 2026b; Leonard and Murray, 2026). Yet these targets largely encode the geometry of the input views, leaving viewpoint changes unsupervised. S-MIND instead supervises its spatial tokens to fuse the views into one frame and to re-express the scene at each viewpoint the reasoning adopts.

sections.title: 3 Does Fine-Tuning Really Internalize Spatial Capability in MLLMs?
sections.content: Higher answer accuracy after fine-tuning does not by itself establish that model has internalized spatial capability. We therefore propose spatial probes, which extend recent analyses of spatial representations in MLLMs (Shi et al., 2026b), to examine what model encodes about scene before and after spatial fine-tuning. They target two capabilities fundamental to spatial intelligence (Cai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b): geometry probe tests whether multiple views are fused into unified internal scene, and viewpoint probe tests whether that scene is transformed to the viewpoints adopted during reasoning. More details are in Appendix A. Finding 1: Limited multi-view fusion. To isolate what the model itself encodes, the geometry probe appends learnable tokens to the frozen model and decodes from their hidden states the 3D point of every visual token, expressed in the first images frame. As Figure 3a shows, on Qwen3.5-4B (Base) it recovers 60.62% of the first images own points (single-view) but only 11.23% of the other images points (fused), which can be placed only by relating the views. Fine-tuning barely closes this gap: the + SFT and + GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) variants lift the fused points only to 14.19% and 16.02%, and the released 3DThinker and GPD reach 10.65% and 11.82%. Crucially, the probes verdict is borne out by behavior. Questions on how the camera moved between two views hinge on exactly this fusion, yet as the top of Figure 3c shows, SFT and GRPO are right on only 53.28% and 56.57% of such questions in MindCube-Tiny, every error placing the second camera on the mirrored 4 Figure 3: Diagnosis of multi-view fusion and perspective transformation in MLLMs. (a) The geometry probe recovers the 3D points of the first image (single-view) and of the other images in its frame (fused). (b) The viewpoint probe reads the relation in the decoded state and directly in the target frame at the first and last mention of the objects, and the scene at the declared viewpoint. (c) The same deficiencies in the answers; mirrored answers place the second camera on the opposite side. Bars are means over models; markers are individual models. side. Overall, multi-view fusion remains persistent challenge for MLLMs, one that current spatial fine-tuning does little to overcome. Finding 2: Incomplete perspective transformation. Shi et al. (2026b) find that base MLLMs fall short in transforming spatial representations across viewpoints. We further use the viewpoint probe to test whether spatial fine-tuning closes this gap: the probe reads the relation between two objects directly in the queried target frame and after an external rotation into it, separating transformation from perception. As Figure 3b shows, the model perceives the scene but largely fails to transform it. On SpinBenchs single-image relation questions (Zhang et al., 2026e), the decoded state gives the correct relation for 95.14% of them once rotated to the queried viewpoint, yet for only 33.44% when read directly in the target frame at the first mention of the objects, and 47.15% at the last. The same holds when the reasoning itself declares the viewpoint: the scene read in the frame of each declared viewpoint is recovered with only 30.02% accuracy on average, barely above the chance level of 25%. The failure is reflected in the answers: as the bottom of Figure 3c shows, the Qwen3.5-4B models reach 85.7198.73% accuracy on questions whose final state lies in the target frame, but only 42.1157.14%, near chance, on the rest. Spatial fine-tuning thus does not close the gap: the scene stays largely anchored to the camera instead of following the reasoning to new viewpoints.

sections.title: 4 S-MIND: Fusing Views, Transforming Perspectives
sections.content: In this section, we detail the two components of S-MIND, each together with its training: multi-view fusion ( Section 4.1), which consolidates the input views into one scene held by compact set of spatial tokens, and perspective transformation ( Section 4.2), which re-expresses that scene in the frame of every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Figure 4.

sections.title: 5.1 Setup
sections.content: Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate S-MIND on four benchmarks, each targeting distinct aspect of spatial intelligence: mental modeling with MindCube-Tiny (Wang et al., 2026b), relational reasoning with SPAR-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025), spatial perception with BLINK (Fu et al., 2024), and perspective taking with ViewSpatial-Bench (Li et al., 2026a). Together, these benchmarks span spatial intelligence from perceiving scene to reasoning about it from viewpoints that no image shows. Following EASI (Cai et al., 2025), we report the accuracy on each benchmark and the average over the four, with the evaluated subsets and the protocol detailed in Appendix C.1. Baselines. Further details of the baselines and their configurations are provided in Appendix C.2. Training Data. All methods trained on our backbone draw on the same three sources, MindCube (Wang et al., 2026b), SpatialLadder (Li et al., 2026d), and SPAR (Zhang et al., 2025). S-MIND uses them in three stages: geometry pre-training on posed image sets from ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) and MindCube, SFT on reasoning chains written by teacher model for questions of the three sources, and RL on multiple-choice question pools built from the same sources and from ScanNet training scenes. Details of the SFT data are provided in Appendix C.3. Implementation Details. We build S-MIND on Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026a), and additionally on Qwen3.5-9B to examine its scalability, with 𝐾𝑠=2 scene tokens per view and 𝐾𝑐=4 camera tokens. We set 𝜆=0.1 and train LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters in all stages. We report S-MIND after its SFT stage and after its RL stage, denoted S-MIND (SFT) and S-MIND (RL). Detailed training setups and parameter configurations are listed in Appendix C.4.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: S-MIND Achieves the Strongest Performance among Spatial Reasoning Models. Table 1 shows that S-MIND built on Qwen3.5-4B reaches an average accuracy of 72.83%, surpassing the strongest method trained in our setting, ProSR, by 7.65 points and the best released spatial reasoning model, Spatial-Interactor-4B, by 17.91 points. The gains are consistent: S-MIND ranks first on all four benchmarks, ahead of the strongest baseline on each by 8.67 points on MindCube-Tiny, 3.10 on SPAR-Bench, 6.25 on BLINK, and 6.44 on ViewSpatial. S-MIND Scales to Larger Backbone and Rivals Frontier General Models. Trained with the same recipe on Qwen3.5-9B, S-MIND reaches 74.03%, 6.76 points above GRPO and 11.76 above SFT, and again ranks first on all four benchmarks, by up to 8.48 points on MindCube-Tiny. As Table 1 shows, compact open model stands on par with frontier general models: at 9B, S-MIND matches GPT-6-Astra, Qwen3.8-Flash, and Claude-Opus-5.5 (73.58%, 73.98%, and 74.15%), and even at 4B it surpasses GLM-5.3-Flash and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (66.23% and 72.06%). S-MIND Is Efficient in Both Inference and Training. Table 2 compares the inference cost of S-MIND with that of SpatialClaw (Cho et al., 2026), an agent on the same backbone that reconstructs the scene and segments objects with external tools, calling the backbone 7.74 times and the tools 4.68 times 9 Figure 6: Analysis of multi-view fusion and perspective transformation in S-MIND. (a) shows the geometry probe on the baselines and S-MIND after SFT (left) and the lead of S-MIND over the strongest baseline on each measure (right). (b) shows the viewpoint probe by the direction of point from the declared viewer (left) and against four controls (right). (c) refits the readout of S-MIND after geometry pre-training at each layer and on the learned mix of all layers (all); vertical lines mark the full-attention layers and dashed lines the level of all. per MindCube-Tiny question. Holding the scene in its spatial tokens, S-MIND needs no tools and answers in single generation: it is 81 faster and 31.05 points more accurate on MindCube-Tiny, and 115 faster and 9.17 points more accurate on ViewSpatial. This efficiency extends from inference to training: as Figure 5 shows, compared with 3DThinker, which also trains geometry into the models states, S-MIND supervises 1,600 fewer values per image, stores 4,400 less supervision data, and trains 19 smaller geometry module, yet it scores 9.97 points higher on average in Table 1.

sections.title: 5.3 Framework Analysis
sections.content: Beyond accuracy, we further examine whether the gains of S-MIND stem from the two capabilities that Section 3 identifies as lacking, namely multi-view fusion and perspective transformation. We first probe whether the model acquires both capabilities and where its backbone fuses the views, then intervene on the spatial tokens to test whether these capabilities causally affect the answers. The Views Are Fused into One Scene. As in Section 3, we retrain the geometry probe on the frozen backbone of S-MIND for fair comparison with the baselines. Figure 6a shows that S-MIND recovers 65.11% of the fused points and 86.32% of the single-view points, whereas the baselines recover at most 16.02% and 60.62%. Cross-view bearing and camera facing improve accordingly, reaching 85.35% and 93.55%. This lead persists as views accumulate: with two images the baselines recover at most 30.28% of the fused points and with eight fewer than 5%, while S-MIND still recovers 50.52% with eight. More importantly, Figure 8b shows that this fusion carries over to the models answers, raising the accuracy on the 274 two-view questions of Section 3, which hinge on relating the two views, from only 53.28% and 56.57% for SFT and GRPO to 96.35% for S-MIND. 10 Figure 7: Interventions on the spatial tokens of S-MIND. Both panels show S-MIND after RL. (a) shows the share of MindCube-Tiny answers that change when the states of the last run of re-emitted spatial tokens are replaced with those of z0, the scene before any transformation, against random perturbation of the same norm; questions are grouped by whether the last viewpoint is an input view (Input) or an imagined standpoint (Imag.), and by setting (Rot.: rotation). (b) shows the lead over the best baseline on each benchmark with and without the spatial tokens at inference. Full results are in Tables 6 and 7. The Scene Turns with the Reasoning. As in Section 3, we retrain the viewpoint probe on the frozen backbone of S-MIND for fair comparison with the baselines. S-MIND reaches 82.17% accuracy, whereas the baselines remain between 25.22% and 37.28%, close to the probes controls. Figure 6b breaks this gap down by direction: all models recover the points ahead of the declared viewer, but the baselines recover at most 10.29%, 9.78%, and 40.69% of those behind it, to its left, and to its right, compared with 77.38%, 69.51%, and 85.29% for S-MIND. The decoded scene is bound to the declaration: as the controls in Figure 6b show, the accuracy falls to 30.10% when another viewpoint of the chain is the target and to 29.43% when the probe reads tokens before the declaration. The Backbone Fuses the Views in Its Middle Layers. The readout leaves the fusion to the backbone by design: its queries carry no image content, and each point query attends only to the scene tokens of its own view and to the camera tokens (Appendix B). To locate where the backbone fuses the views, we take S-MIND on Qwen3.5-4B after geometry pre-training and refit its readout on the states of z0 at one layer at time, scoring it on the 416 ScanNet image sets of the geometry probe. Figure 6c shows that the fused points stay at the level of readout fit on all-zero states through layer 8 (7.6411.12% against 9.21%) and then rise through the middle layers, with their three largest gains, of 12.13 to 14.58 points, at the full-attention layers 11, 15, and 19 of the hybrid backbone. From layer 19 on, every single layer recovers nearly as many fused points as the learned mix of all layers (57.3363.54% against 63.99%), so the fused scene, once formed, is carried through to the last layer. The Answers Depend on the Scene. Decodability, however, does not imply use. We therefore intervene on the RL model at inference, replacing the states of the last re-emitted spatial tokens in its own generation with those of z0. As Figure 7a shows, this state swap changes 9.05% of the answers, mostly from correct to wrong, against only 1.62% for random perturbation of the same norm (Appendix D.1). The effect is strongest where no input image can substitute for the transformed scene: 20.86% of the answers change at imagined standpoints and 28.00% in the rotation setting, whose views barely overlap. Withholding all spatial tokens at inference likewise lowers the four-benchmark average by 2.37 points, from 72.83% to 70.46%. Despite this drop, Figure 7b shows that S-MIND without the tokens outperforms the best baseline on every benchmark, by 5.28 points on average, indicating that the capability is internalized in the backbone, not merely carried by the spatial tokens. 11 Figure 8: Ablation and sensitivity analysis. All variants are built on Qwen3.5-4B and evaluated after SFT on the same data. (a) adds components to text SFT one at time: spatial tokens trained only through the language loss (+ tokens), geometry pre-training and loss on z0 (+ geometry), and the view loss on every re-emitted z𝑘 (+ viewpoint). (b) repeats (a) on the questions that relate the views. (c) varies the geometry weight 𝜆, with the average accuracy at the top and the geometry and transformation readouts below; the shaded band marks 𝜆=0.1.

sections.title: 5.4 Ablation Study and Sensitivity Analysis
sections.content: Geometry and Viewpoint Supervision Each Contribute. Figure 8a builds S-MIND from text SFT one component at time. (i) Unsupervised spatial tokens, trained solely through the language loss, alter the accuracy by at most 1.24 points, indicating that extra tokens and computation alone contribute little. (ii) Geometry supervision, in contrast, yields the largest gain, raising MindCubeTiny from 74.00% to 81.81% and BLINK from 68.25% to 71.75%. (iii) Viewpoint supervision of every re-emitted z𝑘 improves both benchmarks further and is most beneficial on BLINK, whose multiview questions hinge on how the cameras relate, lifting it to 75.00%. Figure 8b further shows the gains on the questions that relate the views: geometry supervision alone lifts accuracy on the 274 two-view questions of MindCube-Tiny from 56.57% to 94.89% and on the 133 multi-view questions of BLINK from 40.60% to 52.63%, which viewpoint supervision then raises to 59.40%. Preserving the Scene Requires Only Small Geometry Weight. Figure 8c varies the weight 𝜆 on the two spatial losses during SFT. Without these losses (𝜆=0), SFT erodes the geometry acquired in pre-training: the 3D points recovered from z0 fall to 48.79%, against 76.13% at 𝜆=0.1. The re-emitted spatial tokens are not transformed either: only 39.85% decode nearest the declared cameras view of the scene in z0, against 97.49%, and 42.55% nearest its view of the true scene, against 96.67%. The average accuracy drops accordingly, to 65.54%, 1.38 points below that at 𝜆=0.1. Any positive weight preserves the geometry (76.1376.41%), but larger weights steadily lower accuracy, from 66.92% at 𝜆=0.1 to 64.01% at 𝜆=1. We adopt 𝜆=0.1, the smallest weight that preserves the scene.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: Conclusion. We introduced S-MIND, framework that internalizes multi-view geometry in MLLMs through compact set of spatial tokens. Our spatial probes first showed that the accuracy gains of spatially fine-tuned models conceal two persistent deficiencies: the views are barely fused into unified internal scene, and this scene rarely follows the reasoning to new viewpoints. S-MIND addresses both by supervising the spatial tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emitting them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks and two model scales, S-MIND achieves the strongest performance among spatial reasoning models, 12 rivals frontier general models, and remains highly efficient at inference. The same probes and causal interventions trace these gains to their source: both capabilities take shape within the model and directly steer its predictions. These results establish internalized multi-view geometry as learnable, efficient, and inspectable source of spatial intelligence in MLLMs. Future Work. We view internalized geometry as cornerstone of spatial intelligence, and S-MIND as one step toward models that think in space. The present work supervises only the geometry that the input views observe. natural next step is an internal scene that reaches beyond these views, completing unseen regions, persisting across interactions, and evolving with dynamic environments, so that the same tokens can support embodied agents over long horizons. As this paradigm matures, spatial intelligence may shift from geometry computed outside the model to property that models carry within themselves, opening research agenda around internal world models, inspectable spatial states, and the joint scaling of perception and reasoning.

sections.title: A Diagnosis Details
sections.content: This appendix details the probes of Section 3 and reports their full results. A.1 Probe Setup In this section, we describe the models we diagnose and the probes we apply to them: Models. Base is Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026a). + SFT is Base fine-tuned with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on reasoning chains written by teacher model, and + GRPO is trained for 375 steps of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with reward on the final answer. They stand for the two common ways of teaching an MLLM spatial reasoning from text and answers alone. We also probe two released spatial reasoning models: 3DThinker (Chen et al., 2026) (its released MindCube checkpoint), built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and GPD (Li et al., 2026e), built on Qwen3-VL-4B. For them, the S-Space axes are those of each models backbone, and each model answers in its own reasoning format, decoded greedily with at most 4,096 new tokens and strict extraction of the answer. Geometry probe. We freeze the whole model and append probe tokens after the images, two per image and four for the cameras. Only the input embeddings of these tokens are trained, together with readout of single cross-attention layer, on posed image sets, with the 3D point behind every visual token and the pose of every camera in the frame of the first image as targets. Whatever is read from the states of the probe tokens was therefore computed by the frozen layers from the images. We then refit fresh readout on the frozen states and score it on 416 held-out ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) image sets, 364 of them with more than one view. We report four quantities. Single-view points are the points of the first image, counted as recovered when they fall within quarter of the sets mean point distance. Fused points are the points of the later images under the same criterion, which can be recovered only by relating those images to the first. Cross-view bearing is the floorplane direction, in four classes, between the points seen at the same grid position in the first image and in another one. Camera facing records whether the optical axis of later camera is recovered within 45. Three controls bound what readout achieves without the geometry, namely shuffling the targets among sets that share source, task, and number of views, setting the states to zero, and replacing the images with gray ones. Viewpoint probe on SpinBench. S-Space (Shi et al., 2026b) finds three linear axes in middle layer of an MLLM along which the positions of objects are encoded. We take the axes of Base at layer 15 and use them unchanged for all three models, so that difference between models is not difference between axes. SpinBench (Zhang et al., 2026e) asks for the relation between two objects as seen from viewpoint other than the cameras, with or without stated premise (144 and 146 questions). On it we compare two answers to the same question: the readout, which decodes the coordinates of the two objects from the state and rotates them to the queried viewpoint outside the model, and the models own answer. We then replay each models own reasoning and read the state at every mention of the two objects. camera-frame readout is right when the state gives the answer after the external rotation, whereas target-frame readout is right when the state gives the answer with no rotation, that is, when the model has already transformed it to the queried viewpoint. This part uses the questions on which the reasoning mentions both objects at least twice, so that the first and the last mention can be compared. Viewpoint probe on reasoning chains. Reasoning chains are teacher-forced through the frozen model, and the probe tokens of the geometry probe, which were never fit to transformed target, are inserted after every viewpoint chain declares. fresh readout is fit to the scene in the frame of the declared viewpoint and scored on 296 held-out chains with 653 declared viewpoints. We score the points that come from the images other than the viewers own by the egocentric quadrant they fall in, as balanced accuracy over the four quadrants. The controls are the targets of the 18 other viewpoints declared in the same chain, the tokens before any declaration, zero states, and targets shuffled among chains. sections.title: B Geometry Readout
sections.content: Figure 10: Architecture of the geometry readout R𝜙. 1 Layer mixing: the hidden states of z0 at all 𝐿 layers are mixed and projected into the keys and values of single cross-attention layer. 2 Geometry decoding: point queries built from the grid position of visual token and camera queries built from the scene tokens of view share this layer. In each row of the layer, the colored tokens are the keys and values that the corresponding query attends to. Linear heads decode the points and poses supervised by Lglobal, Llocal, and Lcam. Architecture. As Figure 10 shows, the readout R𝜙 of Section 4.1 first mixes the hidden states of z0 across all 𝐿 layers of the backbone with learned softmax weights and projects them from the hidden width 𝑑 to 512. The projected states supply the keys and values of single cross-attention layer with 8 heads and width 256, shared by two kinds of queries. The point query q𝑢 encodes only the grid position 𝑢 of visual token, through sinusoidal features at six frequencies and linear layer, and attends to [z(𝑖) ; zcam], the scene tokens of its own view together with the camera tokens. The camera is computed by an MLP from the mean of z(𝑖) and attends to all of z0, for every camera query qcam except the first, which defines the reference frame. No parameter is tied to view index, so the same 𝑖 22 readout serves any number of views. Linear heads map the attention outputs to the global and local points of every visual token, each with confidence 𝑐 = 1 + 𝑒𝑠 from predicted logit 𝑠, and to the floor position and heading of every decoded camera. All coordinates lie in floor-aligned frames, with 𝑥 pointing right, 𝑦 forward, and 𝑧 up, and are normalized by the mean point distance of the image set, as in VGGT (Wang et al., 2025). The readout is deliberately weak, with queries that carry no image content, single attention layer without residual connection, and 1.9M parameters on Qwen3.5-4B and 2.7M on Qwen3.5-9B. The intent is to leave the composition of per-view depth with camera poses to the spatial tokens rather than to the readout.

sections.title: C Experimental Details
sections.content: C.1 Benchmark Descriptions In this section, we describe the four benchmarks used in our experiments: MindCube-Tiny (Wang et al., 2026b) has 1,050 questions over two to four views of scene, in three settings: among (600), around (250), and rotation (200). SPAR-Bench (Zhang et al., 2025) is evaluated on its relational and viewpoint-reasoning tasks (R&V): 11 of its 20 tasks, 3,969 questions, covering spatial relation, spatial imagination, position matching, camera motion, and distance comparison. As in its official overall score, we report the mean of the per-task accuracies. BLINK (Fu et al., 2024) is evaluated on its three spatial tasks, multi-view reasoning, relative depth, and spatial relation, on the validation split (400 questions), whose answers are public. ViewSpatial-Bench (Li et al., 2026a) has 5,712 questions that ask for spatial relations from the perspective of the camera (2,769) and of person in the scene (2,943). Each group is scored by the accuracy over its questions, as in the benchmarks own results. Evaluation Protocol. Every model in Table 1 that we run from its weights answers without thinking mode, with greedy decoding and at most 4,096 new tokens, and Appendix C.2 gives the settings of the general models. The answer is read by strict matching of the option letter in the requested answer format, without an LLM judge, and an answer that cannot be read is counted as incorrect. This follows the protocol of EASI (Cai et al., 2025), and the cited numbers are taken from its public leaderboard1. The average in Table 1 is the mean of the four overall scores. C.2 Baseline Setup In this section, we provide details on the three groups of baselines in Table 1: General models, marked in Table 1, are evaluated through their providers APIs with our prompts and answer extraction, where reply that consists of an option letter alone is also accepted. GPT-6Astra and Claude-Opus-5.5 think at low effort, GLM-5.3-Flash at its default reasoning effort (max), Hy4 and Qwen3.8-Flash run in their default modes via OpenRouter, served by Tencent and Alibaba, and Kimi-K3.1-Pro thinks at low effort and samples at its fixed temperature of 1. The output cap is 32,768 tokens for GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash, 16,384 for Kimi-K3.1-Pro, and 65,536 for Hy4; reply cut at the cap is counted as incorrect. Spatial reasoning models are listed only if their reported numbers are complete or their final weights are released. In the latter case we evaluate the weights () under the decoding above, 1https://easi.lmms-lab.com/leaderboard/, as of July 1, 2026. 23 with their official prompts and formats, except that SpatialLadder-3B and Spatial-Interactor-4B answer our unified prompt. Cambrian-Ss numbers are from the EASI leaderboard. Methods trained in our setting are reproduced on Qwen3.5-4B from their papers and, where available, their official code, on the same training sources as S-MIND. Among them, SFT and GRPO are the key controls: they are trained on the same reasoning chains as S-MIND and differ from S-MIND in the absence of the spatial tokens and their supervision. On Qwen3.5-9B we repeat the comparison with the base model, SFT, and GRPO. C.3 SFT Data Construction In this section, we describe how the data of the SFT stage are constructed: the questions, the reasoning chains, and the viewpoints that the chains declare, which give the targets of the view loss: Question bank. All methods trained on our backbones draw their questions from one bank of 16,808 multiple-choice questions, namely 8,808 questions from the training set of MindCube (Wang et al., 2026b) over two to four views, 4,000 questions of SpatialLadder (Li et al., 2026d) on relative direction and relative distance over single image or eight views, and 4,000 multi-view questions of SPAR-7M (Zhang et al., 2025) in seven task types spanning object relation, spatial imagination, camera motion, position matching, and distance comparison. The questions of SpatialLadder and SPAR come from ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) training scenes. SpatialLadders are sampled round-robin over scenes, with the multi-view direction questions stratified so that no option holds more than 35% of the answers, and SPARs with at most five questions per scene and task type. The boxes and points that SPAR question refers to are drawn onto its images with SPARs official script. All questions share one format: the wording of the source, one option per line, and single instruction to reason first and then answer with an option letter, with every image resized to at most 640 480 pixels. For development we hold out 560 MindCube, 200 SpatialLadder, and 350 SPAR questions by scene, which no training stage uses. Reasoning chains. The reasoning chains are written by GPT-6-Astra. For each question the teacher receives the images, the question as the student sees it, and top-down map of the scene in text: the official layout of MindCube or, on ScanNet, the floor positions and extents of the annotated objects visible in the images together with the camera poses. The student never sees the map. The teacher writes one sentence per viewpoint: each sentence opens with phrase, free of commas, that states where the viewer stands and which way it faces, followed after comma by what is seen from there, and final sentence starting with So draws the conclusion and gives the answer. chain may mention neither the map nor any coordinate, and may use only the numbers that the question and its options contain. chain is kept if its answer is correct and it obeys these rules, and each question is sampled at most three times. Of the 7,824 questions sent to the teacher, 7,500 chains are kept, 2,500 per source. For S-MIND, run of spatial tokens is placed after the first comma of every sentence but the last, i.e., right after each declared viewpoint, without changing the teachers words, and the same chains without spatial tokens are the SFT data of the baselines. Declared viewpoints. The pose of declared viewpoint is position and heading on the floor plane of the first images frame, and the view target is z0s points re-expressed around it: the origin moves to the position and the forward axis to the heading, while heights are unchanged. When the chain adopts the viewpoint of an input image, the pose is that cameras pose as decoded from z0. When it stands at camera but faces elsewhere, the position is the decoded cameras and the heading points to the named object, or follows another cameras decoded heading turned by the stated angle. When it imagines standpoint, e.g., standing at one object and facing another, the position is the first objects and the heading points to the second. The floor positions of objects come from the annotations of the training scenes, scaled to z0s frame, and are the only ground truth in the view target. When it turns relative to where it stands, the previous pose is rotated by 24 the stated angle. The viewpoint is read from the declaring phrase by rules, using only the phrase, the question, and the scenes annotations, never the rest of the chain or the answer, and it serves only as training target: it never enters the models input. C.4 Training Details This section details the three training stages of S-MIND, whose SFT data are described in Appendix C.3. The parameter settings of all stages are in Table 5, and every model is trained once. All experiments are conducted on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Geometry pre-training. The spatial tokens of an image set are placed after the images and before the question. Their input embeddings, the readout, and LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on every linear layer of the language model are trained together on 16,292 posed image sets from ScanNet and MindCube. The readout is described in Appendix B. After training, the readout is refit on the frozen model, and this refit readout is the one that SFT keeps frozen. SFT. SFT starts from the geometry pre-trained model and trains new LoRA on the reasoning chains, whose viewpoint phrases are each followed by run of spatial tokens. The loss is the chains cross-entropy, which leaves out the inserted tokens except the first of every run, plus the geometry loss on z0 and the view loss of every z𝑘 against z0s own scene seen from the declared viewpoint (Appendix C.3), both weighted by 𝜆. Since the first token of every run is predicted, the model learns to write it, and at inference the rest of the run is appended wherever it does. RL. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) starts from the SFT model with fresh LoRA, on multiple-choice questions from the same sources and from ScanNet training scenes. The reward is the correctness of the final answer under strict extraction, with group-normalized advantages and KL penalty to the starting model. The spatial tokens inserted during rollout are context and are not trained. Table 5: The detailed parameter settings when implementing S-MIND. We time SpatialClaw and S-MIND end to end on the same GPU, one NVIDIA H100 PCIe, with eight questions in flight, the default of SpatialClaws official code (Cho et al., 2026). The time of question runs from its start to its final answer, the span that SpatialClaws runner records. SpatialClaw runs its official code in its default configuration: Qwen3.5-4B is served by vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) with thinking enabled at temperature 0.6, and its 3D reconstruction and segmentation tools run on the same GPU. S-MIND decodes greedily as in Table 1, and its accuracies are those of Table 1 on the same questions. As SpatialClaw takes about 100 per question, ViewSpatial is scored on the first 850 of its 5,712 questions in fixed random order interleaving its five tasks in proportion to their sizes. Training cost. Among the methods trained in our setting, 3DThinker (Chen et al., 2026) is the one that also trains geometry into the models states, and its supervision is far heavier than ours. It aligns latent states in the reasoning with the full aggregator features of VGGT (Wang et al., 2025) for every training image, 1,374 tokens of 2,048 channels per image (2.8M numbers), which take 192 GB for our reproduction, through projector of 36.2M parameters. Its latent steps feed the last hidden state back as the next input, which standard serving engines do not support, so its rollouts and its inference decode step by step. S-MIND supervises two 3D points per visual token, global and local, and one 26 pose per camera, at most about 1.8K numbers per image and 44 MB for all 16,292 pre-training sets, through readout of 1.9M parameters, and it runs natively in vLLM.

sections.title: D Additional Experimental Results
sections.content: This appendix complements Section 5 with the state swap, the per-benchmark token knockout, the design choices behind the two supervised stages, and the geometry along training. All runs are single runs (seed 17) on Qwen3.5-4B. D.1 State Swap The swap of Section 5.3 tests whether the answer depends on the content of the transformed scene rather than on the mere presence of the spatial tokens. It runs on S-MIND after RL over all 1,050 questions of MindCube-Tiny. The model first answers greedily with its own reasoning. Its sequence is then cut right after the last run of re-emitted spatial tokens, the run that follows the last viewpoint the reasoning declares, and the model continues greedily from there under one of three conditions, which change the states of that run in every layer and never the text. In the first, the states are left unchanged. In the second, they are replaced by those of z0 at the same layer and position, i.e., the same scene not re-expressed in the declared frame. In the third, they are moved by random vectors of the same norm as that replacement, change of the same size that carries no scene. The last position of the run is left unchanged in all three. sections.title: E A Benchmark for Spatial Capability beyond Answer Accuracy
sections.content: We construct compact benchmark that measures, independently of the answers model generates, how accurately object positions can be read from its representations and whether they follow change of reference view. Figure 14 summarizes the protocol: the model stays frozen, and linear probe reads the position of each object from the hidden state of its name. Scenes. The test set contains 100 scenes, 50 real rooms and 50 synthetic scenes, each with six objects and three views. The real rooms use the RGB views released with SpatialLadder (Li et al., 2026d), with object centers and camera frames from the ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) annotations. The synthetic scenes hold compound objects on platforms and shelves, with partitions, height differences, and partial occlusion, and their geometry and cameras are recorded by the renderer. Objects are identified by name in the real rooms and by the labels AF in the synthetic scenes. Paired inputs. The central comparison presents the same ordered images and object list twice, changing only the instruction from Use image 1 as the reference view to Use image 2 as the reference view, and examines the object pairs whose frontback relation reverses between the two camera frames. Further pairs keep the geometry and reorder the images or the object mentions; synthetic pairs also recolor the objects, relabel them, or move one of them. Readout. Following the object-token readout of S-Space (Shi et al., 2026b), we take the hidden state at the last subword of each object name and fit linear ridge probe to the objects 3D position in the rightupforward frame of the reference camera: bp (𝑟) 𝑖 = 𝑊 eh (𝑟) ℓ,𝑖 + b, (6) where 𝑟 is the reference view and eh is the state at layer ℓ, standardized on the probe-fit set. One probe is fitted per model and domain on 96 real rooms or 300 synthetic scenes; separate set of 20 real rooms or 50 synthetic scenes selects the layer among 3, 7, . . . , 31 and the ridge penalty among 0.1, 1, 10, 100 by mean absolute coordinate error, and the selected probe is frozen for the test scenes. Figure 14: Protocol of the benchmark. The same three views and six object names are presented under two reference-view instructions; frozen model produces the states of the object names, and fixed linear probe decodes their camera-relative positions. The top views show the true layouts of one synthetic scene, in which objects and reverse their frontback order between the two references. The probe is fitted and selected on scenes disjoint from the test set. Physical rooms, including rescans, are disjoint across probe fitting, calibration, and testing. All models receive the same images and instruction, and the input of S-MIND retains its initial spatial tokens. Metrics. Layout error compares the decoded configuration with the true one in the first reference frame. Each configuration is centered and divided by its root-mean-square object spread, and for the normalized configurations b𝑃 and 𝑃 of 𝑛 objects, vt 𝐸layout = 1 𝑛 (cid:13) (cid:13)bp𝑖 p𝑖 (cid:13) (cid:13)2 2 𝑛(cid:213) 𝑖=1 . (7) Reference-view consistency (RVC) is the share of object pairs whose frontback relation is decoded correctly in both reference frames, among the pairs whose true relation reverses and whose coordinate gap exceeds 0.08 of the normalized spread in both frames. Scores are averaged over the eligible pairs of scene and then over scenes. Models and controls. We evaluate five Qwen3.5-4B models: Base, SFT, GRPO, and S-MIND after SFT and after RL. The SFT baseline is an independent reproduction of the recipe in Appendix C.4 (LoRA rank 64, 7,500 teacher-written chains, two epochs). Two controls check the readout: blank images under the fixed probe, and probe refitted on labels permuted across training scenes. The readout follows the reference view. SFT raises RVC over Base from 19.72% to 26.64% on real rooms and from 18.76% to 30.89% on synthetic scenes, whereas S-MIND reaches 35.18% and 44.38% after SFT and 38.10% and 47.26% after RL, 11.46 and 16.37 points above SFT. Its layout error is lower as well, 0.839 against 0.959 for SFT on real rooms and 0.791 against 0.817 on synthetic scenes. Pipeline. Qwen3.5-27B first routes the question in separate pass, given its text, answer choices, and number of images. For visual spatial question, S-MIND receives the question, the choices, and the ordered images, runs once, and returns its spatial analysis with the final answer selection removed. The 27B model then reads this analysis alongside the original inputs, checks the reference viewpoint and the object identities, and produces the answer itself; if the analysis is unusable, it answers from the original inputs alone. Any other question is answered by the 27B model with its original prompt and decoding settings, outside the routing conversation. The spatial analysis transfers to the larger model. We compare Qwen3.5-27B alone and with S-MIND on 64 questions from each of the four benchmarks, sampled by task before inference and aggregated as in Appendix C.1, with thinking disabled, greedy decoding, and at most 4,096 new tokens.
